2027-07-23.title: Friday of the Sixteenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Bridget of Sweden
readings: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery
Lord, you have the words of everlasting life
The seed sown on good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it
2027-07-23.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 16 (Year I). The optional memorial of St Bridget of Sweden, religious, may be kept (white if kept). The psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering (Lectionary 19:8, 9, 10, 11 = NRSV 19:7, 8, 9, 10). Today the first reading is the Ten Commandments, the Decalogue, which the Catholic Church numbers as in the Catechism (CCC 2052–2557). In the month of Karkidakam many Hindu homes in Kerala read a portion of the Ramayana each day; it is a good month to give the Word of God its daily hour. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-23.verse: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; you shall have no other gods before me.
theo: Today's first reading is the centre of the Old Testament: “Then God spoke all these words.” They are given at Sinai, three months after the Exodus, to a people just brought out of slavery. Before any commandment comes a name and a deed: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” The law is not given to slaves to bind them again, but to keep a liberated people in their liberty. In Hebrew the ten are called the Ten Words, and the Catechism teaches that they are a path of life, the “ten words” by which God says to his people what love of God and of neighbour require (Catechism 2056–2057). The Catholic tradition counts them in this way: the first three are about God (no other gods and no idols; the name of the Lord not misused; the sabbath kept holy), and the last seven about our neighbour (father and mother; no murder; no adultery; no theft; no false witness; no coveting of the neighbour's wife; no coveting of the neighbour's goods). The first word is stern because it protects what love is: “for I the Lord your God am a jealous God.” A jealous God is a God whose love wants all of us, as a faithful spouse wants a faithful spouse. The sabbath is not a rule that makes life harder but a gift: a day of rest, in imitation of the Creator, for family, servants, the foreigner and even the cattle. “Honor your father and your mother” is the first commandment with a promise attached, and the one that holds family and society together. The last words go to the heart: “You shall not covet.” The law reaches inside the heart where every sin begins. For Christians, the sabbath rest is fulfilled on the Lord's Day, the day of the Resurrection (Catechism 2174–2176), and Jesus has told us that he came “not to abolish but to fulfill” the law (Matthew 5:17) and that all of it hangs on the love of God and of neighbour (Matthew 22:37–40). The psalm is the sung answer of a people who delight in this gift: “The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul; the decrees of the Lord are sure, making wise the simple … More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey, and drippings of the honeycomb.” We honour the Jewish people, who first received these words and who still cherish the Torah as their delight.

In the Gospel the disciples have heard Jesus tell the parable of the sower, and now he explains it. It is one of only two parables in Matthew's thirteenth chapter that Jesus explains in detail (the other is the parable of the weeds), and he explains it to those who ask. “When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what is sown in the heart; this is what was sown on the path.” The word is heard but never allowed inside. “As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy; yet such a person has no root, but endures only for a while, and when trouble or persecution arises on account of the word, that person immediately falls away.” This is the enthusiast whose joy is shallow. “As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the lure of wealth choke the word, and it yields nothing.” This is the busy person, caught up in worries and wanting more. “But as for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it, who indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty.” In Matthew to “understand” is not only to follow an argument; it is to take the word to heart and put it into practice. Put the two readings side by side. At Sinai God gives the law on tablets of stone; the prophets promised that one day he would do something more: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). The parable of the sower shows how this happens: the word is a seed that must be received into the soil of the heart, where it takes root and bears fruit. The law of the Lord, as Psalm 19 says, revives the soul only when it is received. Today the Church remembers St Bridget of Sweden, a medieval noblewoman, wife and mother of eight children, a widow, a mystic and the founder of an order. Her life shows what good soil looks like: a heart in which the word of God took root, and in which the cares of the court did not choke it. The Church calls her one of the patron saints of Europe.
outline: Ask: if someone asked you for the ten commandments by heart, how many could you give? And which one does your heart find hardest?
Point 1 · The gift before the command
I am the Lord your God, who brought you out: law as a path of freedom.
The psalm of those who delight in the law; love of God and neighbour as its fulfilment.
Point 3 · The seed in the heart
The path, the rock, the thorns and the good soil; the law written on the heart.
A mother, widow and mystic who gave good soil to the word.
“The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul.”
live: Write the Ten Commandments on a sheet this week, and place a small cross beside the one you most need the Lord's help with. Say it in your evening prayer.
Set aside a fixed time each day this week, even ten minutes, for reading the Gospel of the day; put the phone away while you read.
saints: Born c. 1303 in Uppland, Sweden, of a noble family; married at about thirteen to Ulf Gudmarsson and the mother of eight children, among them St Catherine of Vadstena. She served at the court of King Magnus. After Ulf's death in 1344 she gave herself to prayer and penance and began to receive visions that she wrote down (the Revelations); the Church does not oblige anyone to believe private revelations (Catechism 67). She founded the Order of the Most Holy Saviour (the Bridgettines) at Vadstena, approved by Pope Urban V in 1370. From 1349 she lived in Rome, where she worked and prayed for the return of the Pope from Avignon, cared for the poor and pilgrims, and made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land in 1372. She died in Rome on 23 July 1373 and was canonised in 1391. In 1999 Pope St John Paul II named her, with St Catherine of Siena and St Teresa Benedicta of the Cross (Edith Stein), a co-patron of Europe. Her order was renewed in the twentieth century by St Elizabeth Hesselblad, canonised in 2016.
2027-07-23.prayer: Lord our God, you gave your people the ten words on Mount Sinai and wrote your law in the hearts of those who love you. Make us hear your word and understand it; take the stones out of our hearts and cut away the thorns, so that your word may take root in us and bear fruit thirty, sixty and a hundredfold. Through the prayers of St Bridget of Sweden, mother, widow and servant of your word, make us faithful to your commandments, glad in your law and generous to the poor. Lord Jesus, who fulfilled the law by love, write your law on our hearts, and let us love you with all our heart and our neighbour as ourselves. Amen.
altar: At the beginning of Mass we say the Lord, have mercy, because we know that we have not always kept the commandments. At the Gospel we make a small sign of the cross on forehead, lips and heart, so that the word may be in our minds, on our lips and in our hearts. And in Communion the One who fulfilled the law by love gives himself to us, to write the commandments of love in us. St Bridget meditated daily on the Passion of Christ.

quick: At Sinai God speaks the Ten Words, beginning with I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.
The psalm sings that the law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul, and sweeter than honey.
Jesus explains the parable of the sower: the path, the rocky ground, the thorns and the good soil that hears the word, understands it and bears fruit.
2027-07-23.action: Read the Ten Commandments slowly today and pray for help with the one that is hardest for you.
2027-07-23.question: Which kind of soil is my heart when I hear the word of God: the path, the rock, the thorns or good soil?
kidsaint: Bridget lived in Sweden, a country in the cold north, a long time ago. She was a rich lady who married a good man and had eight children. She loved to pray and to think about how much Jesus suffered for us. When her husband died, she gave much of her money to the poor and started an order of sisters and brothers. She travelled to Rome, and then to the Holy Land, where Jesus lived. Lesson: you can be a mother or father and also a saint; what matters is that God's word takes root in your heart.

family.explain: God gave his people ten important rules, the Ten Commandments. They help us to love God and love other people. God said: I am the Lord your God, and I brought you out of slavery. Then he said: do not steal, do not lie, honor your father and mother, and love only God above everything. Jesus said that all the rules are about love. And Jesus told a story about seeds and different kinds of soil: the soil is our heart, and God's word is the seed.
family.intention: We pray for our parents and grandparents, and for people who find it difficult to forgive or to be honest.
family.ask: Ask: “Which rule is the hardest for me? How can we help each other to keep it this week?”

illus: A grocer in a small town in central Kerala hung a small board over his weighing scale: Honest weight, because someone is watching. Customers smiled, thinking it was a joke. One day during the monsoon, when the river road was cut and the shop next door ran out of rice, a woman who had bought from him for years was told by the other grocer that there was nothing left. She walked through the rain to the honest scale. Years later she told her grandchildren: I did not know about God's law then, I only knew that I could trust the man with the scale. His board was a sermon on the seventh and eighth commandments. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord God, you give us your law as a gift. Lord Jesus, write it on our hearts and make us good soil. Amen.
share: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt (Exodus 20:2). How is God's law a gift of freedom in my own life?
The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul (Psalm 19:7). When has a commandment of the Lord given me life?
This is the one who hears the word and understands it (Matthew 13:23). What stops the word from taking root in me?
pm.resp: Lord, you have the words of everlasting life.
interc: For the Church, that she may proclaim the commandments of God as a path to freedom and joy.
For parents and grandparents, who teach the commandments to the young by their lives.
For those who are in prison, bound by sin or addiction, that the Lord who brought Israel out of slavery may release them.
For men and women who read and preach the word of God, that they may be good soil.
For widows, mothers and women of prayer, after the example of St Bridget.
pm.close: Father, you give your law out of love and write it on our hearts through your Son. Keep us faithful to your word and bring us to its fruit. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, the first reading gives us the Ten Commandments. We know them, but listen to how they begin: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery (Exodus 20:2). Before any command, God says what he has done. The law is not the chain of a master; it is the road for people who have just been set at liberty. God says: I have brought you out; now live as a people at liberty. No other gods; do not misuse my name; keep the sabbath; honor your father and mother; do not kill; do not commit adultery; do not steal; do not lie; do not covet.

The psalm sings of these laws as something sweet: more to be desired than gold, sweeter than honey. Do we think of God's commandments in this way? Sometimes we treat them as a list of things we may not do. But a father who tells his child, do not touch the fire, does so out of love. The commandments are the Father's love in words. And Jesus told us that all of them hang on two: love of God with all your heart and love of your neighbour as yourself. If we love, we keep them.

In the Gospel Jesus explains the parable of the sower. The word of God is the seed, and our hearts are the soil. There is the soil of the path: the word is heard but not understood, and the evil one snatches it away. There is the rocky soil: we receive it with joy, but there are no roots, and when trouble comes we fall away. There is the soil full of thorns: the cares of the world and the lure of wealth choke it. And there is the good soil: the one who hears the word and understands it, and bears fruit. It is not enough to hear the commandments; they must be received into the heart, as the prophet says: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).

Today we remember St Bridget of Sweden. She was a wife and a mother of eight, she lived in a royal court, and she was not spared sorrow. And yet the word of God took root in her heart, and it bore fruit in prayer, in service of the poor, in a new religious order, and in a long pilgrimage to Rome and the Holy Land. She shows us that the good soil does not belong only to monks and nuns. Let us ask her to help us, in these rainy days when the land is soft, to make our hearts soft too, and let us give the word of God a fixed hour every day. Amen.
kids: Children, God gave his people ten rules, the Ten Commandments, because he loves us and wants us to be happy and unafraid. They tell us to love God, to respect our parents, not to lie, not to steal, and to be kind. Jesus told a story about a farmer and seeds. Some seeds fell on the road, some on rocks, some among thorns, and some on good soil. The seeds are God's words and the soil is our heart. Let us listen carefully, so that our hearts are good soil, and let us ask St Bridget to pray for us.

intro: Theme: “The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul.”
The gift before the command, the law sweeter than honey, and the seed that must be received into the heart.

sub: I am the Lord your God.
Out of the house of slavery.
Ten words for a people at liberty.
q: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; you shall have no other gods before me.
If you love me, you will keep my commandments.
points.apply: Read Exodus 20:1–17 slowly this week, and thank God for the freedom that the law protects.

sub: More to be desired than gold.
On these two commandments hang all the law.
q: The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul; the decrees of the Lord are sure, making wise the simple;

He said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the greatest and first commandment. And a second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.”
points.apply: Do one act of love for God and one for your neighbor each day this week.

sub: The law written on the heart.
q: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
But as for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it, who indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty.
points.apply: Choose one commandment and ask yourself each evening: how did I keep it today?

points.h: A mother, a widow, a mystic
sub: Delight in the law, day and night.
The thorns of the court did not choke the word.
q: but their delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law they meditate day and night. They are like trees planted by streams of water, which yield their fruit in its season, and their leaves do not wither. In all that they do, they prosper.
As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the lure of wealth choke the word, and it yields nothing.
points.apply: Name the thorn, a worry or a desire, that most chokes God's word in you, and ask St Bridget to pray for you.

concl: God gives his law as a gift to freed people; the psalm sings its sweetness, and Jesus fulfils it in love.
The seed of the word must be received into good soil; St Bridget shows what a heart looks like in which the word takes root.
2027-07-23.resolve: Each day this week give the word of God a fixed hour, and ask the Lord to write his law on your heart.
